bp: Traffic prediction is the everyday problem of estimating how road conditions will change before drivers, buses, delivery fleets, and city services are already stuck with the result. A navigation app, a Web of Vehicles service, or a smart-city control system needs forecasts that fit the shape of the local task: one city may need strong road-network reasoning, another may need careful daily rhythm modeling, and another may need a different mix. The paper is about the work behind building those predictors. It says recent traffic models have multiplied, but many are custom-built structures that transfer weakly when the task changes. ST-LEGO treats model design itself as the object to be predicted and assembled. Instead of asking one human team to invent a new traffic architecture each time, it asks a language model system to read the task, choose reusable structural parts, describe their assembly, and generate executable PyTorch code.
wh: The hard part is not only that traffic changes over space and time. It is that different prediction jobs ask for different balances of the same pressures. Roads influence one another, traffic has repeated time patterns, datasets vary, and the useful architecture for one setting may be too narrow for another. A hand-designed model can be very strong on the case it was tuned for, but the paper says these highly customized structures often have weak transferability. That creates a practical bottleneck: researchers and engineers keep redesigning the outer structure whenever the task changes, even though many pieces are conceptually reusable. At the same time, fully automatic generation is risky because traffic models are not just text. The generated design must have compatible parts, a controlled structure, trainable code, and enough diversity to adapt without becoming an incoherent pile of modules.
naive: A smart beginner might keep a catalog of existing traffic models and pick whichever one performed best on earlier datasets. If the new task looks similar, reuse that whole model; if it fails, tune its settings or add another layer. That is natural because it avoids designing from scratch. It fails for the reason the abstract emphasizes: task heterogeneity. A city grid, highway network, and mixed urban service may need different structural compositions, not just different settings inside the same fixed shape. Another naive path is to ask a language model to directly write a complete traffic predictor from a prompt. That may produce code, but without a standard module library and an intermediate description language, there is little control over whether the structure is reusable, comparable, or consistently executable.
ap: ST-LEGO's central move is to separate architecture design into reusable parts and controlled assembly. The system uses large language models, meaning text-trained systems that can read instructions and produce structured text or code, as modular architects rather than as direct forecasters. A Prompt Agent reads the task requirements. An Assemble Agent turns those requirements into a composition of structural modules chosen from a standardized library. A Code Agent then converts that composition into executable PyTorch code. The important idea is that the model architecture is not treated as one indivisible invention. It is treated as a planned arrangement of pieces, where each piece has a role and an interface. The intermediate structural description language, or DSL, is the controlled recipe between the language model's reasoning and the final code, so generation is flexible without being completely free-form.
mech: The mechanism begins with a traffic prediction task description and the available dataset setting implied by that task. The Prompt Agent translates this request into requirements the system can act on, such as what kind of traffic prediction structure is needed and what modeling complexity must be handled. The Assemble Agent then searches the standardized module library for structural parts that can be combined. A module can be understood as a reusable model component with a known job and a known input-output contract. The agent does not merely name a full model; it builds a structural plan by arranging modules into a larger architecture. That plan is written in an intermediate DSL, a small formal language for describing the architecture before any PyTorch code is produced. This matters because the DSL gives the system a checkable middle layer: the generated design can be controlled, reused, and compared before it becomes code. Finally, the Code Agent translates the DSL description into executable PyTorch. The resulting model is trained and evaluated on real traffic datasets. The paper reports that these generated models show higher accuracy, more structural diversity, and better convergence than many manually designed baselines.
math: The main mathematical idea is compositional search under constraints. Compositional means a large object is built from smaller objects whose roles can be reused. Search means the system must choose which pieces belong together for a particular task. Constraints mean not every arrangement is legal: outputs must feed into inputs, modules must match, and the final design must be trainable. The DSL gives this search a grammar, much like sentence grammar prevents words from being placed in any random order. There is also an optimization idea in the generated predictor itself: after the architecture is assembled, training adjusts numerical settings so predicted traffic is closer to observed traffic. In plain terms, the model repeatedly changes its internal knobs to reduce forecasting error. The language model contributes a different kind of learned mapping: from task descriptions to plausible structural choices. That only makes sense if traffic tasks share recurring building blocks even when their datasets differ. The tradeoff is flexibility versus control. A fixed architecture is controlled but brittle across tasks; unconstrained code generation is flexible but unreliable. ST-LEGO uses modules and a DSL to sit between those extremes.
dots: This paper sits in the conference's broader time-series and spatiotemporal thread, where many papers ask how to predict a changing quantity when nearby places and earlier times both matter. It connects to LLM traffic prediction work such as SMART, which adapts language-model sequence machinery to road networks, but ST-LEGO uses language models at a different level: not mainly to read the traffic sequence, but to design the architecture that will read it. It also neighbors multi-modal traffic prediction work such as VisionST, because both papers respond to heterogeneity. VisionST brings in satellite-image context when historical traffic alone is too narrow; ST-LEGO instead varies the model structure when one hand-built design is too narrow. The shared deeper problem is transfer: how to reuse knowledge across cities, datasets, or tasks without pretending that every traffic setting has the same shape.
ww: ST-LEGO should improve over the naive approach because it preserves two facts at once. First, traffic prediction problems are related enough that reusable parts make sense. Many systems need some way to handle time patterns, spatial relationships, and task-specific complexity. Second, those problems are different enough that a single hand-built architecture should not be expected to fit them all. Modularity lets the system reuse proven pieces while changing the arrangement. The multi-agent split also reduces the burden on any one step. One agent reads the request, one constructs the architecture, and one writes code, so the design process has stages that mirror a human engineering workflow. The DSL is the key reliability bridge: it keeps the assembly explicit before execution. That makes generation less like asking for an unstructured program and more like asking for a valid recipe from known ingredients. The empirical claims in the abstract fit this logic: the generated models are reported to be accurate, structurally diverse, and faster to converge than many manual baselines.
po: The payoff is a more reusable way to build traffic predictors. If the system works as described, engineers can move from task requirements to executable model code without inventing each architecture by hand. The abstract reports gains on multiple real-world traffic datasets: better accuracy, greater structural diversity, and improved convergence compared with many manually designed baselines. That buys practical flexibility for Web of Vehicles services, online navigation, and smart-city applications where tasks keep changing and manual redesign does not scale.
limits: The claims depend on the module library being good enough to cover the important structures in the target traffic tasks. If the right building block is missing, assembly cannot invent it from nothing. The approach also assumes the DSL accurately captures valid model designs and that the Code Agent translates those designs into correct PyTorch. The abstract reports results on multiple real-world traffic datasets, but it does not prove that every new city, sensor layout, or prediction horizon will be covered. It also does not fully show how failures are diagnosed when the language-model agents choose a poor structure.
